entries.test: Whether amateurs using LLM coding tools come to reliably build and run production products that used to need engineering teams, as shown by documented deployments and reliability studies.
entries.note: He repeats his own earlier prediction and stands by it. 'Remotely reliable' is vague, but most readers would test it the same way.

entries.test: Whether there are documented complex real-world apps built mainly by vibe coding that work reliably in production.
entries.note: He states it as a past claim of his that he still holds.

entries.test: Empirical studies of how maintainable AI-generated code is, such as code churn, duplication and technical-debt measures, compared with human-written code.
entries.note: He first made it as a forecast ('would be'). The post restates it as a current fact.

entries.test: Usage, retention and churn data plus customer surveys for vibe-coding platforms in 2025.
entries.note: 'That' points back to all three earlier points, including maintainability, which the proposition leaves out.

entries.test: Web traffic and usage data for the main vibe-coding platforms (e.g. Lovable, Bolt) from early to October 2025.
entries.note: The claim rests on Palihapitiya's chart, which Marcus presents as showing the decline.
This is a broad causal diagnosis ('as always'). Informed readers would choose different tests and reach different answers.

entries.test: Benchmarks or studies that compare how reliably LLMs generate code for common, well-represented tasks versus novel or unfamiliar ones.
entries.note: The hedge 'can be fine' is kept.

entries.test: Surveys or documented case reports of vibe-coding projects, showing how often early success turns into failure or abandonment.
entries.note: 'Often' is vague, but readers would broadly agree on how to test it.
